nameStory: This tiny moth gets its 'orange-headed' name from the striking reddish-orange coloring on its head and the basal area of its forewings. The scientific name 'argenticinctella' comes from Latin meaning 'girdled with silver,' referring to the distinctive silvery lines that border the orange patches on its wings.
description: The Orange-headed Callima Moth is a tiny member of the concealer moth family, with a wingspan of only 10-13 millimeters - about the size of your pinky nail. Its forewings display a beautiful pattern of yellowish-orange with deep reddish-orange patches bordered by distinctive silvery lines with black edges. The hindwings are a duller brownish-gray color, and like other concealer moths, it tends to hold its wings roof-like over its body when at rest.

idTips.label: Silvery wing lines
idTips.description: Look for thin silvery lines bordered with black that create distinct geometric patterns on the orange forewings - these metallic lines catch light and are unique among small moths

idTips.label: Tiny size
idTips.description: Wingspan is only 10-13mm, making it one of the smaller moths you'll encounter - smaller than most people's thumbnail

idTips.label: Orange coloration
idTips.description: Forewings are yellowish-orange with deeper reddish-orange patches that feel velvety to the touch if you can get close enough

idTips.label: Gray hindwings
idTips.description: Hindwings are dull brownish-gray (fuscous) and much plainer than the colorful forewings

idTips.label: Wing position at rest
idTips.description: Holds wings in a triangular, tent-like position over its body when resting, typical of concealer moths

habitat: Found in deciduous forests throughout New England, particularly areas with oak, maple, and other hardwood trees. These moths prefer the understory and forest edges where they can find decaying organic matter and fungi. You're most likely to spot them near fallen logs, leaf litter, or around porch lights in wooded areas.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in April and can be found flying on warm evenings. Look for them attracted to lights during mild spring nights.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with adults commonly seen throughout summer months. They're most active on warm, humid evenings and readily come to artificial lights.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue flying through September and into early October. Late-season individuals may appear slightly more worn with faded colors.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity. The species overwinters in larval or pupal stages hidden in leaf litter and decaying wood.

funFact: Despite being called 'concealer moths,' these tiny creatures are actually terrible at hiding - their bright orange and silver coloration makes them stand out dramatically against most backgrounds, suggesting they may be advertising bad taste or toxicity to potential predators!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small orange micro-moths, but the distinctive silvery lines bordered with black are diagnostic. Remember: 'Silver lines, orange-head' - no other small moth in New England has this exact combination of metallic markings and orange coloration.
contextualKnowledge: Note that some sources may list this species under the genus Epicallima rather than Callima - taxonomists have recently been revising the classification of concealer moths, so you may see both names used interchangeably in field guides and websites.
compareHints: As the only Callima species in New England, compare it with other small concealer moths in the Oecophoridae family. Most other concealer moths lack the distinctive orange and silver coloration, tending toward browns, grays, and muted tones. The metallic silver lines are particularly unusual among this family and make identification relatively straightforward despite the moth's tiny size.
